title: Metacognition
description: Editable version of the complete Mayne Leadership Metacognition course, including its original explanations, practice activities, application, and reflection prompts.
author: Joshua Mayne

blocks.body: YOU
SELF
GROUP
SYSTEM
Think deliberately. Invite dissent. See the system.
Metacognition improves judgment by making assumptions, confidence, social influence, and system effects visible before they harden into decisions.
Four-hour facilitated-course equivalent · Full self-paced adaptation · Progress saved on this device

blocks.title: One discipline. Three levels of thinking.

blocks.body: Individual assumptions enter group conversations. Group decisions alter systems. System feedback then influences future assumptions. The course moves through all three levels before bringing them back together.
By the end, you can
Examine how you form and revise knowledge.
Use practices that reduce groupthink and widen participation.
Move a team from divergence to convergence without forcing false consensus.
Distinguish a visible symptom from an underlying system problem.
Explain not only what you recommend, but how the thinking arrived there.
What am I assuming?Make the hidden frame visible.
Whose voice is missing?Look for social and informational blind spots.
What system am I changing?Trace consequences beyond the immediate event.
Pressure rewards speed. Complexity punishes shortcuts. The pause is not indecision; it is quality control.
Metacognition adds regulation: notice what is happening in your reasoning, name what is shaping it, and navigate toward a better next move.

items.title: NAME
items.text: Which assumption, emotion, source, or pressure is shaping it?

items.title: NAVIGATE
items.text: What should I test, seek, or change before acting?

blocks.body: The purpose is not to eliminate intuition or speed. It is to notice when a fast answer is becoming an untested answer.

blocks.title: Confidence is a feeling. Evidence is a reason.

blocks.body: Who was the 19th President of the United States?

blocks.title: Write a name—or write “I don't know.”
blocks.body: Write a name—or write “I don't know.”

blocks.title: Calibrate your confidence
blocks.body: Record your confidence as a percentage from 0 to 100 before revealing the answer.

items.title: Answer and debrief
items.text:
Answer: Rutherford B. Hayes.

The point is not trivia. Compare your certainty with the quality of the evidence you actually had.

blocks.title: WHAT WOULD HAVE CHANGED MY MIND?

blocks.body: Memory can feel vivid and still be wrong. Social confidence can masquerade as factual confidence. Good judgment includes calibration—matching certainty to the evidence available.

blocks.title: Three forces shape what we accept as knowledge.

blocks.body: Think about a current non-sensitive decision. Rate how strongly each force is shaping your judgment right now.
EVIDENCE
What information supports the claim?
AUTHORITY
Whom or what do I trust in this domain?
CLOSURE
How urgently do I feel I need a settled answer?

blocks.title: WHICH FORCE MAY BE CARRYING TOO MUCH WEIGHT?
WHAT SOURCE OR EVIDENCE SHOULD I CHECK NEXT?

blocks.body: A source can be credible in one domain and weak in another. Urgency can also make the first plausible explanation feel more certain than it deserves.
This is a private reflection, not a diagnostic score. Need for closure can support timely action; the risk appears when the urge to settle suppresses search, dissent, or revision.

blocks.title: URGENCY · How quickly do I feel I need an answer?
RANGE · How many plausible explanations have I considered?
DISCONFIRMATION · What evidence would prove me wrong?
PAUSE · What is the cost of waiting—and of deciding now?

blocks.body: Watch for “seize and freeze”: accept an answer quickly under uncertainty, then defend it after it becomes familiar.

blocks.title: Model revision as strength, not inconsistency.

blocks.body: Think of a belief, judgment, or recommendation you revised.

blocks.title: WHO OR WHAT DID YOU TRUST?

blocks.body: Leadership signal: “Here is what changed my mind.” When leaders explain revision, they teach that evidence can outrank ego.

lessons.title: Invite Dissent and Guide the Group

blocks.body: A team can contain diverse expertise and still produce narrow thinking if the process makes silence safer than contribution.

blocks.title: The absence of disagreement is not proof of agreement.

blocks.body: Select the two pressures most likely to silence useful thinking in your environment.

blocks.title: Two influences suppressing dissent
blocks.body:
Choose two influences relevant to your team.

  • HIERARCHY — The senior person already decided.
  • BELONGING — I do not want to be the difficult one.
  • PACE — We do not have time to reopen this.
  • DOMINANCE — The loudest voice owns the airtime.

blocks.title: WHAT DOES SILENCE LOOK LIKE HERE?
WHAT LEADER BEHAVIOR COULD MAKE CONTRIBUTION SAFER?

blocks.body: Groupthink is not healthy teamwork or legitimate consensus. The problem is premature, protected consensus—when concerns stay private, assumptions go untested, alternatives disappear, and risk looks smaller than it is.

blocks.title: Let the process carry some of the interpersonal risk.

blocks.body: Open all five leader moves, then choose one you could add to a recurring meeting.

items.title: HEAR ALL
items.text: No one speaks twice until all speak once.

blocks.title: THE MOVE I WILL USE
blocks.body:
• Think first
  • Write first
  • Hear all
  • Leader last
  • Use anonymity
Psychological safety develops through behavior over time. Structured facilitation can also reduce the immediate cost of speaking up before that culture is fully developed.

blocks.title: Make the thinking visible before making it final.

blocks.body: 1 · FRAME
What problem are we solving?
2 · DIVERGE
What else could be true?
3 · MAKE SENSE
What patterns and assumptions matter?
4 · CONVERGE
What best fits our criteria?
5 · COMMIT
Who does what, by when?

blocks.title: WHICH STAGE DOES YOUR TEAM MOST OFTEN SKIP?
blocks.body:
• Frame
  • Diverge
  • Make sense
  • Converge
  • Commit

blocks.title: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU SKIP IT?
Productive discomfort is not automatically a process failure.

blocks.body: DIVERGENCEDifferent frames and possibilities expand.
GROAN ZONEConfusion, friction, repetition, integration.
CONVERGENCEShared understanding supports narrowing.

blocks.title: WHAT DOES THE GROAN ZONE FEEL LIKE ON YOUR TEAM?
HOW DO YOU KEEP THE TEAM FROM FORCING A QUICK ANSWER?

blocks.body: Do not rescue the team from productive discomfort by imposing false consensus. Keep participation equitable, the task clear, and the purpose visible.

blocks.title: Imagine the decision failed six months from now.

blocks.body: Scenario: your organization launches a new employee-development initiative. Six months later, participation is low and supervisors say it disrupted operations. Generate three plausible reasons before defending the plan.
Premortems legitimize doubt before people become invested in defending the plan. They separate criticism of a plan from criticism of a person.

blocks.title: Reveal more than yes or no.

blocks.body: Imagine the proposed initiative from the premortem is still being considered. Pre-commit to one position before reading anyone else's view.

blocks.title: Your gradient of agreement
blocks.body:
Choose a position from 1 to 8. The rating opens conversation; it does not replace it.

  • Wholehearted endorsement
  • Agreement with minor point
  • Support with reservations
  • Abstain
  • More discussion needed
  • Do not like, will support
  • Serious disagreement
  • Block / veto if authorized

blocks.title: WHY DID YOU CHOOSE THIS POSITION?
WHAT COULD MOVE YOU ONE STEP?

blocks.body: Use the rating to open the conversation, not replace it. Hear each person once, begin with outliers, and allow revision after the reasoning is heard.

blocks.title: Prioritize. Do not pretend the vote decided truth.

blocks.body: Choose two options you would want the team to analyze more deeply. The vote focuses attention; it does not validate the original framing.

blocks.title: Prioritize two options
blocks.body:
Choose two options for deeper analysis. Voting does not establish truth.

  • Pilot in one unit first
  • Launch to everyone at once
  • Require supervisor sponsorship
  • Offer employee-selected formats
  • Tie participation to real work
  • Use recognition and visible progress
Protect independence by pre-committing before seeing others' votes. After voting, test the leading options against criteria and use gradients of agreement to surface reservations.
A visible incident sits inside a crowded, multi-stakeholder system.

blocks.title: Do not solve the tack incident alone.

blocks.body: A heavily used Northern Virginia trail is experiencing repeated safety problems. Hundreds of bicycle tires have reportedly been punctured by deliberately scattered tacks. At the same time, cyclists, runners, walkers, and inline skaters are competing for limited space on a narrow shared path. Users describe collisions, arguments, different expectations about right-of-way, and disagreement about what the trail is for. Authorities respond to visible incidents, but the broader conflict continues.

VISIBLE EVENT

Repeated tacks and large numbers of flat tires create an urgent safety and enforcement problem.

RECURRING PATTERN

Crowding and conflict among multiple users existed beyond the tack incidents.

SYSTEM QUESTION

How do design, norms, enforcement, capacity, behavior, and stakeholder expectations interact?

blocks.title: Frame before the group influences you.
PROBLEM · State it in one sentence.
STAKEHOLDERS · Who is affected, involved, responsible, or missing?
EVIDENCE · What facts support your frame?
FIRST SOLUTION + ASSUMPTION · What came to mind first, and what assumption sits beneath it?
Preserve different frames before combining them.

blocks.body: Open all four perspectives. Do not decide which is “right” yet. Listen for what each frame makes visible that another could miss.

items.title: CYCLIST / COMMUTER
items.text: Safety, travel time, predictability, right-of-way, and protection from deliberate hazards may dominate this frame.

items.title: RUNNER / WALKER
items.text: Access, physical safety, speed differentials, and the belief that the trail is shared public space may dominate this frame.

items.title: PARK / PUBLIC-SAFETY ROLE
items.text: Capacity, enforcement, cleanup, recurring conflict, rules, infrastructure, and feasible stewardship may dominate this frame.

items.title: SKATER / RECREATIONAL USER
items.text: Access, belonging, skill variation, space needs, and fairness across user groups may dominate this frame.

blocks.title: WHICH FRAME OR STAKEHOLDER DID YOU NOT INITIALLY CONSIDER?
HOW WOULD YOU REWRITE THE PROBLEM NOW?

blocks.body: Select at least three criteria for judging a response.

blocks.title: Criteria for the trail case
blocks.body:
Select at least three criteria and explain their importance.

  • Safety
  • Feasibility
  • Fairness across users
  • Sustainability
  • Unintended consequences
  • Cost / resources
  • Enforceability
  • System capacity
Pre-commit to the two options you would analyze further.

blocks.title: Pre-commit to two response options
blocks.body: Refer to the four options you generated. Record your two leading options before hearing other views.

blocks.title: LEADING OPTION · Which option currently leads, and why?
RESERVATION · What concern remains after narrowing?
WHERE DID YOUR INITIAL FRAME DIFFER FROM YOUR FINAL FRAME?
WHICH VOICE, FACT, OR STAKEHOLDER CHANGED THE CONVERSATION?
WHEN DID YOU FEEL PRESSURE TO CONVERGE?

blocks.body: A decision is stronger when you can explain how alternatives were tested—not only which answer won.
Every fix enters a living system. A useful solution changes the pattern without quietly weakening the system.

blocks.title: Watch for the chain, not just the event.

blocks.body: The original course uses this short systems-thinking cautionary tale. As you watch, capture the original problem, the interventions, the delayed effects, and what the original frame omitted.

blocks.title: WHAT WAS MISSING FROM THE INITIAL FRAME?
A systems lens asks different questions.

items.title: STRUCTURE
items.text: What relationships and incentives produce the pattern?

items.title: MENTAL MODEL
items.text: What assumptions keep the structure in place?

blocks.title: Relief now can quietly weaken the real solution.

blocks.body: Use the bike-trail case—or another non-sensitive workplace issue—to test whether a quick response is masking or weakening a deeper response.

blocks.title: PROBLEM SYMPTOM · What is visible and urgent?
SYMPTOMATIC RESPONSE · What gives immediate relief?
SIDE EFFECT · How might the quick response weaken the system?
FUNDAMENTAL RESPONSE · What changes the underlying conditions?
SYSTEM CAPACITY / HEALTH · What capability must be preserved or strengthened?
DEVIL'S ADVOCATE · Why might the fundamental response fail?
EVIDENCE TO MONITOR · What would show the fundamental response is working?

blocks.body: Shifting the Burden is a hypothesis to test, not proof of causation. Systems thinking without feedback becomes speculation.

blocks.title: The strongest response may combine relief and reform.

blocks.body: STABILIZE NOW
Reduce immediate harm and restore safe operations.
Guardrail: do not let emergency relief become the permanent operating model.

blocks.title: STABILIZE NOW
blocks.body: What immediate response is justified?
BUILD CAPACITY
Change the conditions that recreate the symptom.
Guardrail: define evidence, ownership, resources, and time horizons.

blocks.title: BUILD CAPACITY
blocks.body: What underlying capacity needs to improve?

blocks.title: SUNSET / REVIEW CRITERIA
blocks.body: What prevents the temporary response from becoming permanent?

blocks.title: OWNER + MEASURE
blocks.body: Who owns the transition, and what will they monitor?
Disciplined Decision Map

1. Frame
  2. Diverge
  3. Make sense
  4. Converge
  5. Commit
At every stage ask: What are we assuming? Whose voice is missing? What would change our mind?
Gradients of Agreement

1. Pre-commit privately
  2. Reveal together
  3. Hear each person once
  4. Begin with outliers
  5. Allow revision
Use ratings to open conversation—not replace it.
Shifting-the-Burden Worksheet

1. Problem symptom
  2. Symptomatic response
  3. Side effect
  4. Fundamental response
  5. System capacity
Always add evidence to monitor.
NOTICE
What is happening?
NAME
What is shaping it?
TEST
What else could be true?
ADAPT
What will we change?
SELF
Notice confidence. Name evidence, authority, and closure. Test alternatives. Adapt belief.
GROUP
Notice silence. Name hierarchy and pace. Test through divergence and dissent. Adapt process.
SYSTEM
Notice recurrence. Name structure. Test second-order effects. Adapt intervention.

blocks.title: One decision you will think about differently.
I WILL INVITE A MISSING VOICE BY...
I WILL TEST A QUICK FIX BY...

blocks.body: The quality of leadership decisions depends on the quality of the thinking we make visible. The job is not to eliminate uncertainty. It is to reason responsibly within it.
You examined judgment at the level of self, group, and system—and practiced the tools that keep uncertainty, dissent, evidence, and system effects visible long enough to improve the decision.
